newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Hyundai Electronics sells stake to fund investment.
newsitem.headline: Hyundai Electronics sells stake to fund investment.

text.p: South Korea's Hyundai Electronics Industries, hurting from the plunge in memory chip prices, has decided to sell part of its holdings in a securities house to subsidise investments, company officials said on Monday.

Hyundai Electronics, an affiliate of the Hyundai Group, will sell a 30.93 percent stake in Citizens Investment Trust Management and Securities Co Ltd to Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce for $175 million.
The buyer, the second largest Canadian bank in terms of assets and a leading investment bank, became the single largest shareholder in the South Korean securities house.

But Hyundai Group would remain the biggest shareholder with two affiliates owning a combined stake of 36.86 percent. Hyundai Electronics' stake in Citizens Investment would be reduced to 21.63 percent with the sell-off. Hyundai Securities holds 15.23 percent.

"We decided to make the sale to help finance our investments as long as there will be no problem in owning and managing the securities house," said Kang Seong-soo, finance manager at Hyundai Electronics.
"There were no liquid domestic companies to buy the Citizen Investment stake as many Korean firms are experiencing the same financial shortage we are," Kang said.
Semiconductor companies have served as the cash cows of major South Korean conglomerates, or chaebols, helping to finance expansions at home and abroad.
But excess supply caused memory chip prices to plunge in the past 18 months, reducing Korean makers' margins.
Analysts said Hyundai's move was the right one.

"It's a good decision. Hyundai Electronics has no reason to hold the stake in the loss-making financial institution while the company faces a worsening cash flow," said Bahn Young-won, electronics analyst at Ssangyong Securities.
Kang said Hyundai had planned to invest 1.35 trillion won ($1.5 billion) this year but fell short by 600-700 billion won.
"Even though $175 million will not fully make up the shortage, Hyundai Electronics made the right decision," said Woo Young-moo, electronics analyst at Credit Lyonnais Securities.
Analysts said South Korea's economic slowdown and a slew of corporate failures made overseas financing more expensive.
Woo said the debt-to-equity ratio of Hyundai Electronics rose to 334.7 percent in calendar 1996 from 271.6 percent a year earlier. He forecast the ratio would rise to 370 percent this year.
Hyundai said it would invest 600-700 billion won in thin-film transistor liquid crystal display (TFT-LCD) panels. Another 400 billion won would go to research and development.

The company in May started building a plant capable of processing 360,000 sheets of mother glass per year to make 2.16 million panels of 13.3 inch LCDs. The plant was due to begin full operation in August next year.
LCD panels are mainly used in notebook computers, but analysts said the panels were expected to replace many personal computer monitors in the future.
"Just a few Japanese leaders are making profits in TFT-LCD business. It's not necessarily good news to expand investment in the business," Woo said.
Kang said Hyundai Electroncis would reduce the semiconductor proportion in the company's sales to 50 percent from the current 60 percent.
"Instead, we will beef up our satellite business and related services," Kang said.
He said Hyundai's net profit would rise to 100 billion won in 1997 from 71.14 billion a year earlier.
(Conversion $1 = 891 won)
